chapter: La Rocca on who created jazz
title: La Rocca: jazz was born in Chicago, and attacks on rival bands
summary: La Rocca says the band changed ragtime rhythm in Chicago in 1916, that New Orleans had no jazz, and that Armstrong and the NORK copied the ODJB.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: And they're saying there was some part of the creation of jazz. That Jack Lane, who played a drum and lousy drums at that, created jazz. Now that's good enough for men who thrive on thievery, on a word that we had nothing to do. Our jazz was started in Chicago. We took in the ragtime and changed the rhythm in Chicago. In 1916, we seen we were going to be a flop the first night. And I, being a good dancer, I watched those people. At that time, they had Vernon Castle doing the castle walk. And everybody was trying to copy them. It was a single step. And I'd come to my mind, let me play one of them marches that I played in the carnival parades. And I played the first one. And they went wild. That's when they start howling, jazz it up again. Oh, yes. It was Chicago who nurtured jazz. Not New Orleans. New Orleans knew little about jazz. I came here in 1925. They had no jazz. Even Sharky was imitating Paul Whiteman. All these boys that talked great, whacked so little, did so much. It's easy when a man organized a club to get all his disgruntled musician who never made good to talk against a man who that did made good. And they have proven every word that I have said it be the truth. And that is the truth. I've been told that they had a man come from California, Gus Miller, who played with Paul Whiteman. He played with Tom Brown. He came here to make a tape record. And when he first came in, he wanted to see me. These are his words he put on his postcard. He says, don't let it fool you by me staying with Tom Brown. I always did admire you and I still admire you. But for money, they'd do anything. I've been told that he's been back here under Dr. Sushant's wing to make a tape recording on jazz. Well, all you had to do is listen to him play with Paul Whiteman and his clarinet. And that's what he played for jazz. You listen to all of them. That takes Nunes. That takes them all in. None of them could play the rhythm. The only time they ever played that rhythm was when I was there hitting, beating down on them and carrying them. And otherwise they couldn't play it. And nobody else played it. Hadn't it been from the men from the north. This would have been a lost art. There wouldn't have been no jazz today. There wouldn't have been no other bands like Tommy Dorsey, Artie Shaw, and the rest of them who came up after in the tea gardens from Texas. Where do you think these people learned their music? Like the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. They played six months out here in Chicago. They made a big affair out of it. Well, they had four boys from the north. Do you think these four boys from New Orleans didn't hear the Dixieland Jazz Band? Armstrong says he did. Armstrong came home with arms full of them. And I can prove he styled himself off the Dixieland Jazz Band. And not only that, the need was stolen all the music that I ever composed. They had taken them part by part and tried to recreate something out of something that I had made out of my own brain. When you wrote the book on this jazz of Joe Oliver, you didn't look up any history at all, did you, Mr. Russ?
